sections.heading: Coming to you as I really am
sections.text: Lord, help me come to you with a truer sense of who you are and who I am before you. You live beyond time; my life is brief and small in your sight. The highest heavens cannot hold you; I live in a fragile body, like a clay house. Your power has no limit; I can be undone by the smallest thing. Your understanding is endless; I do not even know myself as I should. You are too pure to approve evil; I have no purity of my own to boast in. Teach me to be honest without despairing, and humble without running away from you.
theological_themes: God is eternal, immense, all-powerful, all-knowing, and holy; the praying person is finite, fragile, ignorant, and sinful.
True prayer begins with a sober view of God’s greatness and human creatureliness, not self-confidence.

scripture_references.connection: This passage holds together God’s eternal, exalted holiness and his willingness to dwell with the contrite. It supports approaching God with both reverence and humility rather than casual self-assurance.
Solomon’s prayer recognizes that even heaven cannot contain God. That directly grounds the contrast between God’s immeasurable greatness and the smallness of human life.
The image of people living in houses of clay emphasizes human frailty. It fits the prayer’s concrete confession that the speaker is not strong, permanent, or self-sufficient.

sections.heading: Asking for the Spirit’s help in weakness
sections.text: In my confusion, weakness, fear, and heaviness, please let your Spirit help me where I am helpless. Give me wisdom where I am blind, strength where I am weak, and comfort where my heart sinks. Do not leave me to manage myself by my own resources.
theological_themes: The Holy Spirit helps believers in weakness and teaches them to depend on God rather than on themselves.
Wisdom, strength, and comfort are gifts from God, not achievements produced by willpower.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that the Spirit helps believers precisely in their weakness, especially when they do not know how to pray as they ought. This grounds the request for divine help in ignorance, fear, and heaviness.
James directs those who lack wisdom to ask God, who gives generously. This supports the prayer’s dependence on God for wisdom rather than self-generated insight.
Christ tells Paul that divine power is made perfect in weakness. That shapes the request for strength as grace received in frailty, not personal toughness.

sections.heading: Letting you search what is really in me
sections.text: Help me look honestly at my life before you. Give me courage to bring hidden things into the light instead of protecting my image. When pressure, disappointment, or temptation exposes me, help me pay attention. Show me what is real, what is shallow, where your grace is growing in me, and where I have been trapped or beaten by sin.
theological_themes: Self-examination is meant to happen before God, with openness to his searching light.
Trials reveal the heart and can expose both genuine grace and remaining sin.
A believer should notice patterns of temptation and defeat instead of pretending they are harmless.

scripture_references.connection: David asks God to search him, know him, and lead him away from grievous ways. This supports honest self-examination as something done under God’s gaze and guidance.

Paul calls the Corinthians to examine themselves and test whether they are in the faith. The prayer’s desire to judge the reality of grace follows this biblical concern for sober spiritual self-awareness.
James teaches that trials test faith and produce steadfastness. This explains why the prayer asks to observe the heart during trials rather than treating trials as meaningless interruptions.

sections.heading: Not trusting myself, but leaning on Jesus
sections.text: Keep me from trusting my own heart. Keep me from resting on old spiritual experiences as if they could carry me today. Keep me from making a big thing of my present promises, as though strong words could make me faithful. Make me strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. When my conscience is guilty, lead me to the cleansing you provide through him; but do not let forgiveness make me comfortable with the sins that still cling to me. Let me receive mercy without making peace with my corruption.
theological_themes: Human self-confidence is unsafe because the heart is deceitful and resolutions are weak.
The believer’s strength is found in Christ’s grace, not in past experiences or present determination.
Forgiveness in Christ gives relief to a guilty conscience while also deepening hatred of remaining sin.

scripture_references.connection: Jeremiah describes the human heart as deeply deceitful. This supports the prayer’s refusal to make the heart, personal sincerity, or present resolve the foundation of confidence.
Paul tells Timothy to be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus. This directly grounds the prayer’s request to be strong in Christ’s grace rather than in self-reliance.

Hebrews teaches that Christ’s blood purifies the conscience from dead works to serve the living God. This supports seeking relief from guilt in Christ’s sacrifice, not in denial or self-justification.
John holds together honest confession of sin and God’s faithful forgiveness. That balance supports the prayer’s desire to receive cleansing without pretending remaining sin is acceptable.

sections.heading: Resting in your mercy and greatness
sections.text: Hold me up in the trials you allow, and use them to change me for good. Give me grace to rest in you while I wait, and steady assurance that you will deliver me in the way and time that are right. Let me never separate your greatness from your mercy, or your goodness from your majesty. When I see you this way, my heart will have reason to praise you again and again.
theological_themes: God sustains his people in trials and uses suffering for their spiritual good.
Christian rest comes from trusting God’s character and promised deliverance.
God’s majesty and mercy belong together; his greatness does not cancel his goodness, and his goodness does not reduce his holiness.

scripture_references.connection: Peter promises that after suffering, God himself will restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish his people. This supports asking God both to sustain the believer and to bring good out of trials.
The psalm calls the soul to wait quietly for God because he is refuge, salvation, and strength. It grounds the prayer’s request for resting in God while awaiting deliverance.
God reveals himself as merciful and gracious while also just and holy. This passage supports the prayer’s desire to hold together God’s mercy with his majesty and his goodness with his greatness.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s strong language of self-abasement could be misunderstood today as denying the dignity of being made in God’s image. I preserved its penitential force while framing it as humility before God’s holiness and human sinfulness, not as self-hatred detached from grace.

The word “depressions” in the original may refer to spiritual heaviness, discouragement, or emotional lowliness rather than modern clinical depression. I rendered it as “heaviness” and “where my heart sinks” without making medical claims.

The request to judge the “reality and degree” of grace can sound like morbid introspection or assurance based on performance. I kept the concern for self-examination but connected it to God’s searching light and evidence of grace, not self-salvation.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Self-noughting” was interpreted as the humbling of self-reliance before God, not the erasure of personhood or denial of creaturely worth.

“Never trust my heart, depend upon any past experiences, magnify any present resolutions” was rendered as rejecting self-confidence, nostalgia, and willpower as foundations for spiritual security, while positively leaning on Christ’s grace.
“Obtain relief from a guilty conscience without feeling reconciled to my imperfections” was interpreted as seeking cleansing through Christ while refusing complacency about remaining sin.
